title: Six Spare MacBook Airs Ran a Private LLM Before Lunch
summary: When our remote development moved to Boxes42, six MacBook Airs with 96 GB of RAM between them had nothing left to do. Finding the right cables took most of the time, Claude Code did the setup, and before lunch one language model was running across all six.
body_markdown:
## Six Macs with nothing to do


Until recently, six MacBook Airs were our team’s remote development machines. Each one ran a Linux virtual machine full of Docker containers, and we worked inside those containers from our own laptops.


Then we moved all of that to[Boxes42](https://boxes42.com/) , the remote development product we build ourselves, and the six Macs had nothing left to do. They ended up on a desk next to mine. Each has an M2 chip and 16 GB of memory.


## 96 GB and an idea


Sixteen gigabytes is not much for a language model, but six of these Macs have **96 GB** between them, which is enough for a fairly large one if they can share it.[EXO](https://github.com/exo-explore/exo) is an open-source tool that splits one model across several Macs, so that each one holds a part of the model and they answer together. I had never tried it, and I wanted to see how it is done.


For that the Macs have to be connected, and the fast way to connect Macs is Thunderbolt. A MacBook Air has two Thunderbolt ports, so six of them can be joined in a line, each Mac cabled to the next. That takes five cables.


## Looking for cables


The cables took **most of the time** . Our office has a drawer full of USB-C cables, and most of them are for charging. They fit the same ports and look much the same as Thunderbolt cables, but they carry little or no data.


I found one that worked and connected the first two Macs with it. I decided to get those two running before I went looking for the other four.


## Handing the setup to Claude


I opened Claude Code, which could reach the Macs over SSH, and handed it the setup. It started by shutting down what the Macs still ran from their days as dev machines, which freed most of their memory, and then installed EXO on both.


The two Macs then ignored each other. Each one decided it was a cluster of one, and nothing said why. Claude went through EXO’s documentation and found the cause in macOS. A privacy setting decides which apps may talk to other devices on the local network, and it was blocking EXO without showing any error. Running EXO as a root system service got around it, and the two Macs found each other within seconds.


At 13:12 the two Macs answered together for the first time, with a small model split in half between them. One of Claude’s test questions asked for a haiku about two laptops joined by a cable:


> Connected in sync
> Laptops merge as one device
> Cord holds them as one


## Four more cables


Then it was back to the drawer for four more. Once they were plugged in, two of the five links did not work.


Macs 5 and 6 saw each other only as plain USB devices. A MacBook asks “Allow accessory to connect?” when something new is plugged in, and nobody had clicked Allow, because nobody uses these laptops anymore. I walked over and clicked it.


The link between Macs 4 and 5 showed a cable plugged in and no data at all. Claude compared it with the links that worked and concluded that a charging cable had made it past me. I swapped it. Claude could see both problems from inside the Macs, and I fixed them by hand.


## One download instead of six


The model for all six Macs was Qwen3-30B-A3B, which takes about 16 GB. That is too big for any one of these laptops, which was the point.


EXO has every Mac download the whole model, even though each one uses only a sixth of it. Claude suggested downloading it once and copying it to the others over the cables, and I said no and let EXO do it its own way.


Twenty minutes later one Mac had the whole model, the others were still downloading over the office Wi-Fi, and the slowest had 80–90 minutes to go. I asked Claude to do what it had suggested. Copying the model from that one Mac to the other five over Thunderbolt took **about 30 seconds** .


## Before lunch


At **13:54** the model answered from all six Macs, each one holding a sixth of it. Claude’s test asked for a haiku about six laptops joined in a line by cables:


> Six laptops line up,
> Cables weave a digital thread
> Silent, shared thought.


It wrote about 20 tokens a second, faster than I can read, and it listed the first 40 prime numbers correctly.


*Every Mac showing EXO’s dashboard with all six nodes connected.*


The six laptops nobody needed now sit on the desk next to mine, joined by five cables, running a language model that does not fit on any one of them. The model runs entirely on those six machines, so nothing anyone asks it leaves the office. Then I went to lunch.


## What you can do with it


If you have a few spare Apple silicon Macs, you can run a private language model on them. EXO counts about 50 GB of free memory across our six. Models up to about 45 GB should fit, which means up to about 80 billion parameters at 4-bit.


Short questions get quick answers. A long document takes a minute or more before the first word appears, because the model reads the whole prompt before it writes anything.


More Macs let you run a bigger model, but they do not make it faster, because every token passes through every Mac in the line.


EXO serves an OpenAI-compatible API on every Mac, so most tools that work with the OpenAI API can use the cluster once you point them at it.

## Frequently asked questions


### Can you run one LLM across several MacBooks?


Yes. EXO, an open-source tool, splits one model across several Apple silicon Macs so that each one holds a part of it. I ran a 30B model (Qwen3-30B-A3B, about 16 GB at 4-bit) across six MacBook Airs with 16 GB each. It does not fit on any one of them.


### How fast is a 30B model on six MacBook Airs?


About 20 tokens a second, with the first words after about a second for short questions. Long prompts take longer to start, because the model reads the whole prompt before it writes anything. A long document can take a minute or more before the answer begins.


### Why did my Macs not see each other in EXO?


In my case the macOS Local Network privacy setting was blocking EXO from talking to the other Macs, without showing any error. On a Mac you can click on, allow EXO under Local Network in System Settings. On Macs you only reach over SSH, running EXO as a system service as root fixed it, and the Macs found each other within seconds.


### How big a model fits on six 16 GB MacBook Airs?


EXO counts about 50 GB of free memory across six of them, so models up to about 45 GB should fit, which means up to about 80B parameters at 4-bit. More Macs let you run bigger models, but they do not make a model faster.
